ἐκ τοῦ — κληθῆναι in L, where K indicated a lacuna to be filled with the explanation of the name Priapus : ἰδοῦσα δὲ ἡ Ἀφροδίτη οὐκ ἠξίωσεν ἀναλαβέσθαι, τά τε ἄλλα μισήσασα τὸν παῖδα καὶ διὰ τὸ ἀπρεπὲς τοῦ αἰδοίου (from scholion b). διὰ οὖν τὸ τὴν Ἀφροδίτην ἀπαρνηθῆναι τὸν παῖδα ἐκεῖ Ἀπαρνὶς ἡ πόλις ἐκλήθη in P

10 Etymologicum Genuinum (AB) Πιτύεια: it is a headland near (παρὰ in A) Lampsacus. And Pityeia was formerly called Lampsacus because it had many pines. Apollonius I 933. Stephanus of Byzantium Λάμψακος: a city on the Propontis ... formerly called Pityousa, as Deiochus of Cyzicus (fg 10 M. II 19). Epaphroditus (fg 29 Luenzner) says that Pityeia was called by Homer this name because it had an abundance of pines, being called Laomedonteia. sch. B B 829 Eust. 355, 42 Strab. XIII 588
11 Πιτύουσαν in Stephanus of Byzantium : Πιτύαν in F : Πινύαν in L : omitted in P. These were supplied by K from a similar passage.

Aparnis is a place on the Hellespont, which in ancient times was called Aparnis, as has been said, from Aphrodite, having given birth to Priapus there, renouncing the child because of the unseemliness of his genitals.
4 ἡ δὲ Ἀβαρνίς — αἰδοίου in L : omitted in this place in P (see note on scholion a)

There is a steep island: The Propontis is the sea after the Hellespont, after which comes the Thracian Bosporus. In this Propontis there is an island, which later became a peninsula and had a certain isthmus; for every land projecting into the sea is called an isthmus. Near this peninsula lies Mount Arcton, properly so called, since they say that the nurses of Zeus, spending time there, were changed into bears; or because the place is full of wild beasts, and it was named from the animal, the bear; or because of the height of the mountain, from its seeming to approach the celestial bears. This mountain was inhabited by certain wild Earth-born men. The peninsula itself and the isthmus were inhabited by the Doliones, whose king was Cyzicus.

The sequence is as follows: there is a high island in the Propontis, a short distance from Phrygia along the stream of the isthmus, lying close to the land above the Aesepus river, having shores on both sides; and it is called Mount Arcton.
